name: gRPC
summary: An interface-defined RPC framework that turns service methods into generated client and server APIs over unary and independently flowing streaming calls with deadline and cancellation lifecycles.

features.name: IDL-defined service boundary
features.description: gRPC defines services and RPC methods in an interface definition, using Protocol Buffers by default for service and message descriptions. The fixed C++ generator emits client stub and server method interfaces from method descriptors.
benefits: Generates matching client and server API surfaces
Separates transport invocation from application implementation
costs: Participants couple to generated APIs and serialization
Generated APIs expose language-specific lifecycle details

features.name: Unary and streaming call shapes
features.description: gRPC supports unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidirectional-streaming methods. The fixed C++ generator selects distinct reader and writer interfaces for the streaming combinations.
benefits: Preserves order within an individual RPC stream
Allows independent read and write progress in bidirectional calls
costs: Streaming needs lifecycle, buffering, and backpressure reasoning
Generated method variants expand the API surface

features.name: Deadline-bounded call lifecycle
features.description: gRPC lets clients specify a deadline and documents DEADLINE_EXCEEDED on expiry. The fixed core Call stores a send deadline, propagates the minimum parent deadline, and cancels the call when the deadline expires.
benefits: Nested calls inherit a no-later-than parent bound
Timeout behavior is explicit in the RPC lifecycle
costs: Client and server can reach different local success conclusions
Cancellation does not roll back already-applied work

features.name: Generated transport-facing stubs
features.description: The gRPC programming model presents a local client stub whose methods wrap request messages, perform remote calls, and return response messages. The fixed C++ generator emits synchronous, asynchronous, callback, and streaming method declarations.
benefits: Makes remote methods look like typed local APIs
Offers blocking and asynchronous execution styles
Aligns message construction with the service definition
costs: Local-looking calls retain network failure semantics
Several execution styles increase generated API complexity
Channels and call contexts remain application concerns

mathematical_views.question: How does one service definition connect method signatures to generated client and server boundaries?
assumptions: Each method has one request and response type
Generated interfaces preserve the declared method shape
Transport details are abstracted behind generated APIs

mathematical_views.question: How can an RPC represent independently progressing client and server message sequences?
assumptions: Each direction has an ordered sequence within one call
No cross-direction order is inferred without application rules

mathematical_views.question: Which call transitions remain possible before a deadline and what terminal outcome follows expiration?
assumptions: A call has a deadline and can be cancelled
Nested propagation takes the minimum bound
Local termination is distinct from remote work

costs: Schema and generated-code compatibility require coordination

benefits: One framework covers unary and sequence protocols
costs: Streaming adds buffering and termination complexity

benefits: Bounds remote wait and inherited work

costs: Generated APIs expose several concurrency models
